figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: PhotoGuider turns a whole scene into a framed photograph and provides a reasoned explanation for its choice of framing. The four stages follow what a photographer actually does upon arriving at a scene: look around, settle on a direction, adjust the frame, and press the shutter. (1) Given a 360° panorama, the system scans look directions and (2) scores each using the proposed four photographic tokens: Subject, Composition, Integrity, and Aesthetics. The maximum fixes the camera direction. (3) The frame is then refined within that view, and (4) the final photograph is rendered natively from the panorama. The same four tokens also ground the explanation: our MLLM explainer is fine-tuned to cite these tokens and conditioned on their measured assessments. Below, two results show the selected crop and the produced explanation; phrases grounded in the four assessments are highlighted.
figures.headline: The pipeline scores look directions with four tokens, takes the maximum as camera direction, refines the frame, and renders it natively.
citing_sentences: The overview of PhotoGuider is demonstrated in Fig. 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: One set of photographic tokens, three uses. Each token yields one assessment score for a given frame, allowing the decision layer’s output to be separated into four interpretable metrics. These drive our entire pipeline by (1) scoring all view directions in a 360° scene, (2) ranking shortlisted framings and gating each refinement step, and (3) anchoring the fine-tuned MLLM’s explanations. An optional generalist MLLM acts only as a consultant during refinement.
figures.headline: The same four tokens score view directions, rank framings, gate refinements and anchor explanations.
citing_sentences: The method and training overviews are shown in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3, respectively.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The three learned components of PhotoGuider. We use single ground-truth crops from FCDB and top-rated crops from GAICD, with labels defined by the overlap (IoU) between candidate framings and reference crops. (1) Ranker. Candidates are scored using four LightGBM models (two regression and two ranking) operating on two feature tiers: a 17D core set (saliency, geometry) and a 60D full set (adding SAM object semantics, aesthetic scores, and CLIP prompts). Blending these model outputs yields three quality scores ($q_{A},q_{B},q_{C}$) to determine the optimal crop. (2) Refinement Gates. Six LightGBM gates adjust the selected crop by predicting IoU gains: one gate recenters the frame (via rule-of-thirds and CLIP-attention), four evaluate expansion (based on subject coverage, composition, scale-aesthetic variance, and golden ratio alignment), and a final gate shrinks the frame if no expansion triggers. (3) Explainer MLLM. It generates explanations conditioned on the crop, measured geometry, and ranker attributions. Training data drafts are filtered via four strict quality checks (unmasked geometry, numerical consistency, feature citations, and vocabulary validity).
figures.headline: Three learned components are a ranker, Six refinement gates, and an explainer trained on filtered drafts.
citing_sentences: The method and training overviews are shown in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3, respectively.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Feature Partitioning and Token Definitions. The four tokens partition the 60 extracted features into disjoint subsets. Each reported score represents one such component, expressed as a percentile against the same quantity derived from training crops that match the human annotations most closely. The assessed frame is highlighted by the yellow box.
figures.headline: The four tokens partition the 60 features into disjoint subsets, each reported as a percentile against matched training crops.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Examples from PhotoGuider on FCDB (Chen et al., 2017a) and FLMS (Fang et al., 2014) testing images. Green boxes are ground-truth crops from both datasets, and yellow boxes show crops from PhotoGuider. Bottom-right: IoU between the predicted and ground-truth crops.
figures.headline: PhotoGuider's crops on FCDB and FLMS testing images are compared against ground-truth crops, with IoU printed for each.
citing_sentences: The example crops from PhotoGuider are shown in Fig. 5.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Visual comparison of 360° view framing from the Poly Haven HDRI library. Score heatmaps are produced by each method across 120 look directions (24 pan × 5 tilt). Scores are displayed as percentile ranks, with red denoting highly favored directions and a star marking the peak score, alongside the corresponding rendered photograph. Each panel labels the chosen camera parameters (pan / tilt / field of view) and shows the percentage of participants who rated it first. Across 100 scenes, the first-place preference shares are 19.5%, 27.3%, and 53.2%, respectively.
figures.headline: Score heatmaps over 120 look directions for three methods, labeled with first-place shares of 19.5%, 27.3%, and 53.2%.
citing_sentences: Qualitative comparisons among the three methods are demonstrated in Fig. 6.

figures.caption: Dataset Bias from FCDB and FLMS datasets. Each point is one crop selected by PhotoGuider, positioned by the contributions of two of the four photographic tokens. Normalized by the pooled standard deviation, the median-to-median displacement is 0.34 SD in the S-A plane and 0.47 SD in the C-I plane.

abstract: Traditional image cropping assumes the photograph already contains the composition worth keeping, and asks only where to crop. A full 360° scene offers no such guarantee: the viewing direction in a scene has to be discovered before anything can be framed. We present PhotoGuider, a measure-then-frame method that answers both questions with compact learned scorers over one shared set of composition-aware features. The designed features are extracted using foundation and task-specific vision models and structured into four photographic tokens: Subject, Composition, Aesthetics, and Integrity. Our MLLM explainer is fine-tuned to generate composition-related explanations conditioned on images and measured token assessments. To our knowledge, PhotoGuider is the first method to combine explicit composition-based direction selection in 360° panoramas with refined framing, camera-parameter output for native re-rendering, and measurement-conditioned explanations. On two standard 2D cropping benchmarks, PhotoGuider achieves the highest average mIoU performance against ground-truth crops. In a blind ranking study, 120 participants ranked three cropping methods over 100 panoramic scenes from the public Poly Haven HDRI library, placing our framings first in 53.2% of cases, against 27.3% and 19.5% for two strong alternatives. Project page: https://ntuneillee.github.io/research/photoguider/

sections.body: The paper argues that a 360° scene requires choosing a viewing direction before a frame can be formed, while existing 2D croppers assume a pre-shot photograph. PhotoGuider scores candidate frames with four tokens, Subject, Composition, Integrity, and Aesthetics, computed from pre-trained vision models. The stated contributions are composition-aware cropping with a ranker of only 63k parameters, and an MLLM explainer conditioned on token assessments and geometric measurements. The MLLM is confined to a consultant role that neither scores nor makes decisions. This section does not report experimental results.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Panoramic framing needs a direction choice before cropping, which PhotoGuider addresses with four interpretable photographic tokens.

sections.body: The section reviews four areas: hand-designed and generate-and-rank croppers, end-to-end regressors, MLLM-based croppers, and aesthetic critique generators. It notes that fixed objectives in end-to-end methods make scoring evidence difficult to inspect, and that free-form MLLM rationales receive limited checks against measurable image properties. For 360° view selection, it says saliency alone is insufficient for aesthetic view selection and that existing view scores lack interpretability or conflate framing with camera-pose objectives. It also covers interpretable decision layers, including generalized additive models and gradient-boosted trees, which the decision layer draws on. The section contains no experiments.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior croppers, critics, and view selectors offer scores that are hard to inspect or check against measurements.

sections.body: Candidate framings come from eight sources, and a determinantal point process selects ten diverse framings, of which the top three go to the main ranker. Four tokens partition 60 features: Subject (10D), Integrity (20D), Composition (22D), and Aesthetics (8D). Ranker tiers use a 17-dimensional core set and a 60-dimensional full set. Gate models then decide three spatial moves: recentering, expansion, and shrinking, each firing only when predicted IoU gain exceeds a threshold. For 360° scenes, a coarse stage picks the highest-scoring look direction, and a fine stage reprojects it and outputs pan, tilt, field of view and aspect ratio.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: PhotoGuider ranks shortlisted candidate framings with four photographic tokens, then refines the top frame with gated moves.

sections.body: On FCDB and FLMS, PhotoGuider full mode reaches an average IoU of 0.811 and an average BDE of 0.044, while fast mode reaches an average IoU of 0.797. The token ablation names Subject and Composition as the strongest single groups, and all four tokens together give the best cropping performance. The fine-tuned explainer lowers the detector-measured contradiction rate of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 6.31% to 1.55%. In a double-blind study of 50 participants, PhotoGuider's explanations received 40.0% of 250 votes, against 32.8% for Venus and 27.2% for ArtiMuse. The 360° study used 120 participants, 100 scenes, and 4,820 rankings, comparing PhotoGuider with Venus and CACNet.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: PhotoGuider's full mode scores highest average mIoU, 0.811, on two 2D benchmarks and places first in 53.2% of 360° rankings.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that PhotoGuider uses four interpretable tokens to drive a compact ranker, a gated refinement module, and an explainer, and reports competitive performance on two benchmarks. It cites user evaluations showing preference for its crops over end-to-end and MLLM baselines. The first stated limitation is that framing adjustments use discrete step fractions, so targets between sampled intervals are only approximated. The second is that view selection uses a single argmax, returning one frame even in scenes with several strong regions, regardless of user preference. Future work will examine continuous refinement and user-guided view selection.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors list discrete refinement steps and a single view argmax as limitations.

sections.body: The appendix defines the 60 measured features and their grouping into Subject, Composition, Aesthetics, and Integrity, and explains how TreeSHAP attributions are summed per token. It lists the eight candidate sources in Table 4 and the gated recenter, expand, and shrink rules. It gives consultant settings of m=5 temperature-sampled decodes and M=4 paraphrases, and explainer training with QLoRA at r=16 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Module ablation reports mIoU rising from 0.754 to 0.759 on FCDB and from 0.820 to 0.835 on FLMS with full refinement. User-study analysis reports a Friedman statistic of 43.4, Wilcoxon tests, and a bootstrap 95% CI of [48.8%, 57.6%] for the 53.2% share.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists token feature definitions, candidate sources, gate details, consultant and explainer settings, and user study analyses.
